sourceEvidence.title: Front Coil Spring Fracture Causing Tire Contact and Loss of Control Risk
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect both front coil springs for rust scaling, broken lower coils, abnormal ride height, and tire sidewall contact marks. The proper repair is replacement of both front springs, and often the strut assemblies or spring seats if corrosion is advanced; alignment should be checked afterward. In rust-belt cars, inspect the opposite side even if only one spring has failed.

sourceEvidence.title: Intermittent No-Start or Engine Stall from Faulty Crankshaft Position Sensor
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnosis typically involves scanning for crank/cam correlation or crank sensor circuit faults, monitoring live RPM during cranking, and checking sensor wiring near the engine for heat or connector issues. If the signal is erratic or absent, replacement of the crankshaft position sensor and inspection of the harness/connector is the usual repair. Clearing codes and confirming a stable RPM signal on restart completes the fix.

sourceEvidence.title: Timing Belt Neglect Leading to Bent Valves and Sudden No-Start on 1.6L Engines
sourceEvidence.howToFix: If the engine cranks unusually fast, has no compression, or died suddenly, inspect timing belt integrity and cam timing immediately. Preventive service is critical: replace the timing belt, tensioner, and idlers on schedule, and many owners also replace the water pump and front seals at the same time. If the belt has already failed, a compression or leak-down test is needed to determine whether valves were bent.

sourceEvidence.title: P0303 — Cylinder 3 Misfire from a Failed Ignition Coil (Most Common) or GDI Carbon/Plug Wear
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Swap the cylinder-3 coil with an adjacent cylinder — if the misfire moves, replace the coil; if it stays, inspect/replace the spark plug. On higher-mileage GDI engines address intake-valve carbon with a walnut-blast cleaning, then test the injector and do a compression/leak-down check. Typical coil-and-plug repairs run modest; injector or carbon work costs more.

sourceEvidence.title: Ignition Coil Pack Failure Causing Misfire
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace failed ignition coil(s). Replace spark plugs at the same time. For 2004+ models, consider replacing all four coil-on-plug units as they tend to fail in sequence. Use NGK or Denso quality replacements.

sourceEvidence.title: Weak A/C Cooling from Condenser Leak / Compressor (TSB Build-Date Range)
sourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose with a system pressure/leak (dye or electronic) test. Recharge only after the leak is found. Leaking condensers are replaced (often the cheaper fix); a failing compressor requires compressor, orifice tube and receiver/dryer replacement plus a system flush if debris is present. Apply the relevant A/C performance TSB for in-range build dates.
